Hi @drmobasher — the `DEPRECATION:` line you posted is a **warning, not an error**. With pip 23.2.1 the install still goes ahead. Here's what it means, why it happens, and how to install cleanly.

### 1. What is wrong

`aizynthfinder[all]` depends on `route-distances`, which requires `pytorch-lightning>=1.6.0,<1.8.4`. Most releases in that range declare their torch dependency like this:

```
torch (>=1.9.*)
```

That is not a valid version specifier.

### 2. Why it is wrong

Python packaging versions follow a standard ([PEP 440](https://peps.python.org/pep-0440/#version-specifiers)). The `.*` wildcard is only allowed with `==` and `!=`:

- `torch==1.9.*` is valid and means "any 1.9.x".
- `torch>=1.9.*` is invalid. "Greater than or equal to a wildcard" has no defined meaning.

Older pip versions guessed what was meant. Current pip follows the standard strictly. It **skips** releases with invalid metadata instead of guessing, and the warning you saw announces that change.

### 3. How to install it correctly

Use a fresh virtual environment with Python 3.10–3.12 (aizynthfinder doesn't support 3.13 yet):

```
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install "aizynthfinder[all]" "pytorch-lightning==1.6.5.post0" "setuptools<81"
```

Why each step:

- **`--upgrade pip`:** a current pip handles this case correctly and avoids the warning.
- **`pytorch-lightning==1.6.5.post0`:** this is the release in the allowed range with valid metadata. A current pip picks it automatically; pinning makes it explicit.
- **`setuptools<81`:** this old pytorch-lightning imports `pkg_resources`, which recent setuptools no longer ships. Without the pin, the install succeeds but `import pytorch_lightning` fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pkg_resources'`.

Check that it works:

```
python -c "import route_distances.route_distances; print('ok')"
```

### 4. Why this is not a pip bug

pip is applying the packaging standard that all Python tools share. The invalid metadata is inside the pytorch-lightning 1.6–1.8 release files on PyPI, and published files can't be changed afterwards. The lasting fix belongs upstream: `route-distances` should allow a newer `pytorch-lightning` (later releases have valid metadata). That's worth reporting to the route-distances / aizynthfinder maintainers.

If the install still fails after these steps, please post the **complete** output, especially any lines starting with `ERROR:`. The warning alone doesn't show what actually went wrong.

I think this is a consequence of pip respecting the max cache age of the HTTP response from the API server (https://github.com/pypa/pip/pull/13955) that was introduced in pip 26.2.

I believe this is working as intended, the same behavior would happen if the users access was revoked server side, pip would have no way to know that authentication was revoked. Equally, I don't think it makes sense that pip monitor every possible way an HTTP request might go out differently, and therefore affect authorization, there are a lot.

If you wish pip to have the old behavior, of making a new API request on every invocation, you can run with ` --refresh-package=:all:` (the option is per-package if you want to be more specific), or permanently set with `pip config --user set global.refresh-package ':all:'`.

Either way the cache responses will exist on disk, if you no longer wish unathenticated responses or distributions to exist on disk after running `rm ~/.netrc` run `pip cache purge`.

@peterjc  I suspect the cause is the `actions/cache` step in your `linux_prep` job that saves the whole `${{ env.pythonLocation }}` directory, site-packages included (not pip's own cache, which only holds downloads).

The likely sequence: `setup-python` provided a Python whose bundled pip was already 26.2.x, then your cache step restored a snapshot from when it still had pip 26.1. The restore is a tar extraction over the live directory: it overwrites files in the archive but deletes nothing. pip 26.2 renamed `pip/_internal/build_env.py`  to a `build_env/` directory and moved `get_runnable_pip` to `utils/misc.py`, so you'd end up with 26.1's files plus a leftover 26.2 `build_env/` directory.

A package shadows a same-named module, so 26.1's `main_parser.py` would import 26.2's `build_env/`, which looks for `get_runnable_pip` in 26.1's `utils/misc.py`, where it doesn't exist. If that's right, it was old pip importing new pip, not the reverse.

Your cache key hashes `pyproject.toml` and `ci-dependencies.txt`, so a pip bump in the runner image never invalidates it, and a future pip release that renames a module could reproduce this. Adding the bundled pip version to the key, or not caching `pythonLocation`, would avoid it.

The responsible commit is 5c9ec602159d5d2b03fe32e63614925287b1b0d3 which is indeed the build isolation work. The `venv-isolation` feature is experimental and opt-in, but there was a separate bugfix included in that change. Previously, the pip install subprocess used to install build dependencies wasn't isolated from the outer environment, but in 26.2 that was fixed since it was needed for `venv-isolation` to work.

The leaky isolation was mostly OK because we currently use `--ignore-installed` while installing build dependencies (but `venv-isolation` doesn't) and it had the extra benefit of allowing the pip subprocess to use the keyring from the parent environment.

In the meanwhile, you can use a different experimental feature which doesn't use subprocesses to install build dependencies: `--use-feature=inprocess-build-deps`.

I'll issue a hotfix in the coming days. (Which IMO feels a bit much, but we have issued hotfixes for seemingly any unintended regression and this counts.)

Actually, the other easier workaround is to activate the virtual environment so pip will find the same keyring instance when the import provider fails and it falls back to using the keyring available on PATH. (I realized this while trying to write a test for this.)

Sigh, alright this ended up being way trickier than I initially assumed:

- Yes, we should revert this bugfix for the default isolation method.
- However, there's no good way of fixing this when `venv-isolation` is enabled because it invokes the pip subprocess using the temporary venv's Python executable (by design), so the parent venv's keyring will never be able to be imported. 
- The proper fix for both cases is stop calling pip in a subprocess to install build dependencies, but sadly, there is more work left before we can enable `inprocess-build-deps` and `venv-isolation` together (which is the end goal).

I agree that `--no-require-hashes` is an useful addition as an escape hatch from pip auto-enabling `--require-hashes` if a single hash is provided. It's plausible that people will want to only hash-lock a selection of requirements (say all packages from PyPI, but none from their local corporate index).

I previously wrote a few paragraphs explaining that commit-locked VCS requirements should still work even if `--require-hashes` is enabled, but then I realized that VCS dependencies (with a revision specifier) are legal in standard dependency metadata. Some people probably do rely on that if they use hashing checking at all, then they will be only consuming hash-locked distribution files. This is a nice property for security since it prevents issues where (A) hashes are forgotten for one package OR (B) if for whatever reason a new dependency is pulled in (for example, because the deployment platform changed and an OS/Python gated dependency is now needed).

I'm still leaning towards supporting VCS requirements even with `--require-hashes`, but it isn't as simple as I previously thought. Realistically, I don't think scenario (B) is what `--require-hashes` is really meant to protect against. If it really is a concern, then `--no-deps` ought to be used, too. 

TL;DR, I think adding `--no-require-hashes` and possibly supporting commit-locked VCS requirements with `--require-hashes` are both useful features and if anything, orthogonal to each other. On a more practical matter, `--no-require-hashes` is much simpler than the latter.

Alternatively, https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/4995#issuecomment-594142084 is always an option, but no one has offered to research the original context for why `--require-hashes` is automatically enabled when a `--hash` option is provided. Without that, I'm afraid that the ship has long since sailed and `--no-require-hashes` is the safer approach.

@archer-cmd  what you're describing isn't a `pip uninstall` flag it's the job of a project / dependency manager. `pip` is currently an installer: it works on a flat environment and doesn't record why each distribution is there.
 
To reap orphans safely you need both the dependency graph and the set of packages you explicitly requested. `pip` doesn't have a project API so can't act safely here.

Every tool below supplies that model:
 
> manifest (top-level deps) → lockfile (resolved graph) → a `sync` step that prunes anything extraneous.
 
---
 
## TL;DR
 
| Tool | Remove a package | Prune orphans / sync env |
|---|---|---|
| pip-tools | edit `requirements.in` | `pip-sync requirements.txt` |
| uv | `uv remove X` | `uv sync` |
| Poetry (≥2.0) | `poetry remove X` | `poetry sync` |
| PDM | `pdm remove X` | `pdm sync --clean` |
| Pipenv | `pipenv uninstall X` | `pipenv clean` |
| Hatch | edit env deps | `hatch env prune` (+ recreate) |
| pipdeptree | *inspect only* | `pipdeptree --reverse` to find orphans |
 
---
 
## Project / workflow managers (declare → lock → sync)
 
### pip-tools
`requirements.in` holds your top-level deps; `pip-compile` resolves them to a pinned `requirements.txt`; `pip-sync` makes the environment match it exactly, uninstalling anything not listed.
 
```bash
pip install pip-tools
pip-compile requirements.in      # -> fully pinned requirements.txt
pip-sync requirements.txt        # env := requirements.txt exactly (orphans removed)
```
 
> `uv pip sync requirements.txt` is a faster drop-in for `pip-sync`.
 
### uv
`pyproject.toml` declares top-level deps; `uv.lock` pins the full graph; `uv sync` makes the venv exactly match the lock (removes extraneous packages by default — `--inexact` to keep them).
 
```bash
uv add requests
uv remove requests       # drop from pyproject.toml, re-lock, prune orphans
uv sync                  # venv := uv.lock exactly
```
 
### Poetry (≥ 2.0)
`pyproject.toml` declares; `poetry.lock` is the resolved graph; `poetry sync` ensures the locked deps are the only ones present.
 
```bash
poetry add requests
poetry remove requests   # removes the package + deps no longer needed
poetry sync              # env := lockfile exactly (was `poetry install --sync` pre-2.0)
```
 
### PDM
PEP 621 `pyproject.toml` + `pdm.lock`. `pdm sync --clean` removes packages no longer in the lock.
 
```bash
pdm add requests
pdm remove requests
pdm sync --clean         # prune packages not in pdm.lock
```
 
### Pipenv
`Pipfile` + `Pipfile.lock`. `pipenv uninstall` edits the `Pipfile`; `pipenv clean` uninstalls everything not in the lock.
 
```bash
pipenv install requests
pipenv uninstall requests
pipenv clean             # uninstall anything not in Pipfile.lock
```
 
### Hatch
Environments are declared in `[tool.hatch.envs.*]` and built in isolation, so an env only contains what its config implies — "recreate to match" rather than in-place pruning, but the effect is the same.
 
```bash
# edit [tool.hatch.envs.default] dependencies, then:
hatch env prune          # remove built envs; next run rebuilds from declared deps
```
 
---
 
## Finding orphans by hand
 
### pipdeptree
Not a remover — it renders the installed dependency tree (and the reverse tree), which is how you spot orphans before `pip uninstall`-ing them yourself.
 
```bash
pip install pipdeptree
pipdeptree --reverse --packages requests   # what still depends on requests?
```
 
Until pip provides it's own sync command or project API, there are plenty of other choices here.

After digging into the codebase, I was able to pinpoint the root cause. The culprit is `SimpleWheelCache.get()` in `src/pip/_internal/cache.py`, which has no special handling for local directory links. When the package name is known from the specifier (e.g. `Red-DiscordBot @ file:///path/to/dir`), it finds a matching cached wheel and returns it without ever building from the local directory.
Adding the following check at the start of `SimpleWheelCache.get()` fixes the issue:
```python
if link.is_existing_dir():
    return link
```

@pfmoore thaks for the quick response and for being open to a PR. About the threat model point, the scenarios where modifying the sidecar is not equivalent to modifying the wheel are ones where this would matter: 

* **S3-backed indexes:** bucket policies routinely apply different ACLs to .metadata files versus .whl files, because .whl files are considered high-value and .metadata files are considered low-risk metadata. An IAM key with PutObject scoped to the bucket can overwrite sidecars without touching wheels. The wheel hash on the index page still points to the original unmodified wheel and passes. 
* **CDN cache poisoning**: .metadata files are small (mostly few kbs) and get cached aggressively at edge nodes. An attacker who can poison a CDN edge cache for a specific .metadata path serves tampered metadata to everyone behind that CDN without touching the origin. The wheel is served from origin and its hash passes. 
* **Artifactory/Nexus blob stores:** the index is generated from a database, the artifacts live in a blob store. A misconfigured storage policy or compromised service account can write to the blob store without any access to the index database or wheel files. 

In these cases the attacker cannot change the wheel, the wheel is protected by a separate access control boundary. The sidecar is the only thing they can touch. These are where the sidecar has a different exposure surface than the wheel, making the reconciliation check valuable as exactly the belt-and-braces validation you mentioned.

Having sat on our pylock story for a little while, this is where I'm at currently:

- Supporting `-r pylock.toml` as just another source of requirements is logically consistent and does enable some advanced workflows. Given pip's role as a package installer (and not a project workflow tool), I don't think it's unreasonable to support these use-cases by virtue of not treating `pylock.toml` specially in `pip install`, at least in the interim as we still figure out the whole `pylock.toml` support story.
  - On the front of not treating `pylock.toml` specially, for example, using a lockfile as a constraint file is obscure, but at first impressions, seems like an useful feature: https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/13961. We should wait for more interest before seriously considering the feature, but it's not _useless_.[^2]
- _However_, I still maintain that `pip install -r pylock.toml` should NOT be the primary way people should consume lockfiles. They ought to use `pip sync` unless they're doing something bespoke or advanced that needs that all of the features of `pip install`. Sure, they may "just" be better `requirements.txt` files, but the main point of a lockfile is be able to set up a reproducible environment. It should be easy to do that [without shooting yourself in the foot](https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/13952#issuecomment-4328728968). a `pip sync` should avoid most of the configuration knobs that `pip install` has, including `--only-final` and `--all-releases`, while having different defaults, like `--no-deps`.
- In the future, we ought to strongly recommend using `pip sync` over `-r pylock.toml` in our documentation and communications. It's also possible that we remove or restrict what `-r pylock.toml` does[^1]. 

[^1]: although, I get the feeling this won't be possible due to pre-existing use already
[^2]: FTR, Charlie suggested supporting `-c pylock.toml` before pip even gained `-r pylock.toml` support: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/13031

You’re very likely hitting a user/system mismatch (multiple Python installs on Windows). Please run these in PowerShell and compare the paths:

Which Python is running:

```powershell
python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
```


Which pip is tied to that Python:

```powershell
python -m pip --version
```

Which pip version is on PATH:

```powershell
pip --version
```


The two `pip --version` commands should point to the same director* and the same Python version. If they don’t, you’re installing with one pip and running another Python.

What executables are on PATH:

```powershell
where python
where pip
```

If you see entries in both `Program Files\Python...` and `AppData\Local\Programs\Python...` (or `AppData\Roaming\Python...`), that confirms multiple installs.

Where are packages being installed:

```powershell
python -m site
python -m pip show pip
```

If those paths don’t line up with `sys.executable`, that’s the issue with your environment.

I took a quick look at pip's source code and I don't have any clue on what causes `PIP_EDITABLE` to bug.

The problem is that pip is picking up this `-e .` requirement when it's calling itself to install build dependencies in the isolated environment used to build your project. If that's confusing, this is what is happening:

- You run `PIP_EDITABLE="." pip install`
- pip prepares to install the local directory as an editable
- pip sets up a temporary build environment for this project
- **pip installs the build backend and any build dependencies (as configured in `pyproject.toml`) in this environment**
- pip calls the build backend to create an editable install for this project
- pip installs the file the build backend generates

It's in step 4 (bolded above) where things go wrong. To install build dependencies in the isolated environment, pip calls itself. This pip subprocess picks up the `PIP_EDITABLE` environment variable and then tries to go through the exact series of steps as noted above. This will recursive infinitely. The install ultimately fails because pip notices the recursive build and stops execution, thinking you're installing a fork bomb or similarly malicious project.

The good (ish) news is there is a solution in the works. In pip 26.0, we've shipped a new alternative flow for build dependencies where they are installed within the same root pip install process. This avoids the new pip subprocesses and weird option inheritance. This feature is still experimental, but it can be enabled with `--use-feature=inprocess-build-deps`. If you pass this flag to pip, the install does complete without issues.

The bad news is that pip 26.0 is extremely new so I'd imagine you probably can't rely on it. We do plan on switching to this new mechanism wholesale eventually, but today is not that day yet. Sorry!

* A supply chain attack is found in a popular package, but it is older than most users have set their cooldown to, it is removed and new version of a package is added for users to safely upgrade to

This is intended behaviour, and matches the spec for version matching. It was implemented when we updated our vendored version of the packaging library in 25.0. From the changelog for that version:

> The inclusion of packaging 24.2 changes how pre-release specifiers with < and > behave. Including a pre-release version with these specifiers now implies accepting pre-releases (e.g., <2.0dev can include 1.0rc1). To avoid implying pre-releases, avoid specifying them (e.g., use <2.0). The exception is !=, which never implies pre-releases.

This is highly surprising to me. And there seems no alternative now to specifying compatibility with multiple major releases but with an upper bound.

8.0.0 is not the smallest possible 8.x release, that is 8.0a0. But that now triggers release candidate inclusion for 7.x versions.

`~=` can only be used for a single major version and can also not be used to require a certain bugfix release for the lower bound and allow other minor releases.
This will work for all pip versions and not select pre-releses by default: `astropy<8.0.0,>=6.1`.

Hey, sorry if the above comment was a bit short and mysterious, I was at work but wanted to give you a practical answer. Here is  a more detailed explanation:

You are correct that `8.0a0` is less than `8.0`, although you are incorrect it is the smallest possible `8.x` release, that would be `8.0dev0`.

However, Python packaging specifiers, especially when it comes to pre-releases, do not act like their counterpart less than and greater than operators. There are two relevant sentences in the spec[^1] , firstly:

> The exclusive ordered comparison <V MUST NOT allow a pre-release of the specified version unless the specified version is itself a pre-release. 

That means given `<8.0` then any version which is a pre-releases of `8.0` must not be selected, e.g. `8.0a0`, secondly:

> Allowing pre-releases that are earlier than, but not equal to a specific pre-release may be accomplished by using <V.rc1 or similar.

This means that given `<8.0rc1` you must allow any pre-release version smaller than `8.0rc1`, e.g. `8.0a0`.

Now, because these two lines were right next to each other they were easy to confuse them and think that `<V` never implies accepting pre-releases, and for a long time it was implemented incorrectly in [packaging](https://github.com/pypa/packaging/), and therefore pip.

This does allow pre-releases to be implied in more situations, but given the above your use case is neatly satisfied by using the specifier `<8.0` which does not allow pre-releases of `8.0` and does not imply selecting pre-releases.

I am going to close this issue as working as intended, but please let me know if you have any more questions.


[^1]: https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/version-specifiers/#exclusive-ordered-comparison

Reflecting what I said on the CPython issue, I think the pip RM should create the PR for CPython to update ensurepip to the latest version of pip. Thats an entirely non-controversial change, because the policy for ensurepip is simply to have the latest available version of pip embedded. CPython's policy on PRs is that they need to be linked with an issue, and we've historically simply created an issue saying "Update pip to version X.Y", matching the PR with the same title. I think that's an entirely reasonable thing to ask of the pip RM, and should remain our standard process.

If there's an existing CPython issue that's relevant, as in this case, I think it's fair for the pip RM to decide on a case by case basis whether to link the PR to that existing issue or not. If they prefer not to, the CPython core devs can review the existing issue independently and decide whether the ensurepip upgrade fixes it or not.

Personally, in this specific case, I'd have been willing to link the pip PR to the existing issue, based on @hugovk's recommendation. I would *not* have assumed that made pip in any way responsible for claiming that "upgrade ensurepip to use pip 26.0.1" was the right fix for that issue, nor would I have had any concerns about checking the status of the CVEs involved. That's something that I'd expect to have been thrashed out on the issue *before* we were asked to link the PR to it. But @notatallshaw is the RM, and he's entitled to make whatever judgement call he prefers on the matter - link to the existing issue, or raise our own issue. The only thing I don't think is reasonable is to not create the PR - that's always been the pip maintainers' responsibility and I think it works better if it remains as such.

One thing I will offer - *if* @notatallshaw has serious reservations about the existing process, and wants to start a discussion about changing it, to the point where he's not willing to create the CPython PR for 26.0.1, then I'll create that PR and we can have the discussion without delaying the ensurepip update. Variant plugins should not have any information from the resolver, otherwise there is no way to apply any kind of logical inference from resolution states in the solver, for example if `a=1 b=1` is unsatisfiable at any point, then it should remain unsatisfiable, no matter what changes about the rest of the resolver state. `variant_properties` doesn't depend on the current active state of resolution no.

`variant_properties` is effectively a set of strings that is an intersection of the set of strings from the wheel artifact itself and the output of the plugin (that runs prior to resolution) that indicates what variants are compatible with the current system.

So given you have a variant that indicates what ABI of pytorch you're running against, you might end up with 3 variant wheels.

```
foo-1.0-Variant1
  - Valid for `"abi::torch::2.8.0"`
foo-1.0-Variant2
  - Valid for `"abi::torch::2.7.1"`
foo-1.0-Variant3
  - Valid for `"abi::torch::2.7.0"`
```

All 3 of these wheels have the following metadata:

```
Requires-Dist: pytorch==2.8.0; "abi::torch::2.8.0" in variant_properties
Requires-Dist: pytorch==2.7.1; "abi::torch::2.7.1" in variant_properties
Requires-Dist: pytorch==2.7.0; "abi::torch::2.7.0" in variant_properties
```

If someone runs `pip install foo`, then the following would (in the hypothetical that variants land) happen:

1. During collection, pip would invoke the pytorch abi provider, which would say that this system is compatible with `{"abi::torch::2.8.0", "abi::torch::2.7.1", "abi::torch::2.7.0"}`.
2. Pip would see those 3 variants, see that they're all compatible with the current system and collect all 3 of them.
3. Resolve, picking whichever one of them it saw first (let's say it's Variant1, which depends on `pytorch==2.8.0` through the environment markers).
4. Install foo 1.0 (Variant1) and pytorch 2.8.0.

However, the fact it selected Variant1 was just due to that one being "first", all 3 variants were equally valid.

So what if instead the user ran `pip install foo pytorch==2.7.*`? The following would happen:

1. During collection, pip would invoke the pytorch abi provider, which would say that this system is compatible with `{"abi::torch::2.8.0", "abi::torch::2.7.1", "abi::torch::2.7.0"}`.
2. Pip would see those 3 variants, see that they're all compatible with the current system and collect all 3 of them.
3. Resolve, picking whichever one of them it saw first (let's say it's Variant1, which depends on `pytorch==2.8.0` through the environment markers).
4. Throw a resolution error.

In the latter case, if pip didn't lump all 3 variant wheels together and reject all 3 because one of them failed, then (4) would be successful, because pip would reject Variant1, then move onto Variant2, and the marker evaluation would say that it depended on `pytorch==2.7.1`.

It has nothing to do with variants getting information into or out of the resolver, and it's not even really specific to variants at all. The generalized problem is what do you do when there are multiple wheels that can satisfy `foo==1.0` and the _effect_ of selecting one of those wheels over the other changes the ultimate set of dependencies to be installed.

The easiest (maybe only?) way to have this happen today is to have two wheels, that are valid for the current platform+python version, with different `METADATA` files that have different `Requires-Dist` entries, but I think you can run into it mixing `py3` and `cpXY` wheels and environment markers. In any case, this case will be more _likely_ with variants, because in most cases projects do not have overlapping wheels like that currently.

Another way of thinking about it is that currently pip assumes that the effect on the dependency graph of selecting `foo-1.0` will be the same regardless of which wheel you select, so `foo-1.0` is effectively the "node" for the dependency graph. Solvers like `uv` already know this isn't the case when they're attempting a universal solve, because selecting a windows wheel might pull in different dependencies than selecting a linux wheel, so they fork the resolution for those cases (they're using environment markers instead of wheels themselves, but that's immaterial here).

This is my biggest problem with the current state of the wheel variant proposal, that it assumes it's OK for resolvers to backtrack into wheel selection in the way that you're describing here.

As @notatallshaw says, the existing specs say nothing about the process of resolution, or about how to interpret multiple requirements. And I think that's a good thing - we *don't* want to over-constrain what algorithms tools use. I'm not saying that pip *couldn't* change how it handles resolution, but it would be a major change, and a significant disruption. Furthermore, I'd be pretty cross if the standard disregarded the realities of pip's current implementation, and didn't justify such a significant chunk of work.

To inform the wheel variant proposal, and for context here, the following (simplified) explanation of how pip resolves a set of requirements is probably sufficient to expose the underlying problem. This should be taken as "how things are", and not as an invitation to debate ways in which the model pip uses can be changed. I'd love to see a similar summary from uv, and from other resolvers. I guess they could be very different because of the "universal resolution" mechanism.

1. Pip resolves a set of requirements by considering "candidates". There is precisely one candidate for each name/version involved in the resolution process.
2. Candidates are specific distribution files - a wheel or sdist.
3. Candidate selection happens independent of resolution. You can think of it as happening first, although in practice it happens "on demand". But there's no way to feed information from the resolver back into the candidate selection process (the "finder" in pip's terms).

The crucial point is that last one. You *have* to pick the wheel you intend to use without reference to the resolution process. I agree with the point that @pradyunsg made that it would be useful to make the selection process deterministic (if it isn't already), but that will still only be by statically inspecting the available distribution files for a name/version and choosing one.

To be clear on if you are affected by the CVE:

* CVE-2025-8869 is a specific instance of CVE-2007-4559, which is that a tarfile archive can be extracted with a link that points outside the archive
* CVE-2007-4559 was fixed by Python >=3.9.17, >=3.10.12, >=3.11.4, or >=3.12, so if you are on one of Python versions you are not affected by CVE-2025-8869, if you are not on one of those Python versions you are not on a secure version of Python
* CVE-2025-8869 affects building/installing source distributions (sdists), not installing binary distributions (wheels), the building of an sdist can already run arbitrary code
* No pip version has yet been published on PyPI which mitigates this CVE, but I see several redistributions of pip (e.g.https://github.com/wolfi-dev/os/pull/67721), which presumably offer extra support, are starting to include the patch directly

From my perspective as a the person who merged the PR (https://github.com/pypa/pip/pull/13550):

* Pip doesn't have a support policy for insecure versions of Python, although maintainers have accepted patches on a best effort basis
* The PR was reasonable outside the security angle, these tarfiles are invalid if they point to things not inside them
* The security angle, **in my opinion**, is dubious, as building sdists already involves arbitrary code execution, so I find it hard to come up with a scenario where someone cares about tar extraction pointing outside the archive but doesn't care about the arbitrary code execution

I was therefore not planning to create a pip release based on this PR, and I'm still not as it would be my first release of pip and I don't have capacity right now if I make any mistakes or have to do a follow up. However, I am not against another maintainer cherry picking this patch and doing a release if they want, but please be aware all maintainers of pip are currently here on a volunteer basis and so it requires they have the spare time and will to do so.

Actually, now understanding the flow a little better this is working as intended, pip does the following things when collecting wheels:

1. Check the filenames match the current environment (OS, python version, etc.)
2. Check the Requires-Python matches the current Python

In the case of torch the filenames are more specific than the Requires-Python and therefore `--python-version` makes a difference but `--ignore-requires-python` doesn't. However, for packages that are the other way around, where the filenames are quite liberal but the `Requires-Python` are not then `--ignore-requires-python` does make a difference, e.g. https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/13579#issuecomment-3288725299

This two step process is a little confusing, but it is an artifact of the spec, I'm not sure pip can really do anything about it.

For what it's worth, the pip project does not collect any telemetry. What we do is collect system/python environment information and send it over as part of the User Agent which may or may not be collected by the remote index. In practice, pip's user-agent is formatted for ingestion by PyPI's linehaul service and PyPI is the most commonly used index.

I'm fine with documenting what the average pip user would be revealing through telemetry, but it is at risk of falling out of date when PyPI updates their policies (like whether they store IP logs, etc. etc.). Also, by inspecting the tags of the wheels, the remote index can still (w/o the user agent) infer a handful of system properties (architecture, OS, and Python version) when a platform specific wheel is used.

Fair enough, in terms of extracting requirements from a `pyproject.toml` there are a few main issues with adding this to pip as I know it:

This only works for completely static dependencies from a PEP 621 spec compliant configuration, if there are dynamic dependencies this will have to fail or result in installing the wrong thing. That's why https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/11440 is considered a better solution, it can get the correct dependencies in all situations.

Users have multiple existing workarounds. For example, running install and then uninstall e.g. `pip install foo`, `pip uninstall foo`). Or by extracting the dependencies themselves, e.g. `python -c "import tomllib;print(*tomllib.load(open('pyproject.toml','rb'))['project']['dependencies'], sep='\n') > .temp; pip install -r .temp"`, this could be made a one-liner if https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/7822 is implemented.

Also, a proper UX would need to be designed, personally I don't think hijacking the existing `-r` flag is the best approach, now [dependency groups](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/user_guide/#dependency-groups) have been implemented I would expect a similar UX to extract dependencies and additional dependencies. Somebody needs to design and implement this in a way where the maintainers are happy.

FWIW I am not against this, but I do think actual real use cases should be provided, you've said that you want to install dependencies but not the project, but why? And why are workarounds not sufficient? And why would it not be better served by https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/11440? The justification is required partly because pip is currently an all volunteer project, maintainers only have a very limited about of time to review PRs and support features.

> For starters, I don't think anyone assumed pyproject would be as popular as it is now

On the contrary, `pyproject.toml` was defined as the standard for project metadata, so it's not surprising it's used everywhere. What *has* changed is that people are using it for projects that aren't intended to be built into a redistributable wheel. That's not the originally intended use, and as of now such usage hasn't been standardised (although there have been some discussions, such as [here](https://discuss.python.org/t/projects-that-arent-meant-to-generate-a-wheel-and-pyproject-toml/29684)). Feature requests like this come mainly from that usage.

In situations like this, where there are no established standards, pip deliberately avoids innovating on behaviour. That sometimes means that we are slow to adopt emerging conventions, but that's fine - people who want more innovative approaches can use one of the existing workflow tools like uv, PDM, Poetry or hatch.

The problem with "simply" allowing pip to read dependencies from `pyproject.toml` is that the semantics of the `[project.dependencies]` metadata isn't necessarily appropriate for a standalone project. Restrictions that are needed when building a wheel can be problematic for a standalone project. For example, it's not possible to specify a dependency on another local project (in a directory on your machine) because that's not portable - but it's a common need for standalone projects. Hence the reason this needs to be properly discussed and agreed in a tool-independent way - it would be a nightmare if you had to specify such things one way for pip, a different way for uv, yet another way for PDM, etc...

I have no idea what the likely timescale is for standardisation. Tools like PDM, uv, Poetry and hatch have good real-world experience to bring to the discussions, but standardisation takes time, and everyone involved is a volunteer, so we're dependent on people having an interest in the working on the subject. And right now, interest in metadata for standalone projects seems to have died down.

#11440 and #8049 were both opened a while ago and there have been at least two new PEPs, along with support in pip:

[PEP 735 Dependency Groups in pyproject.toml](https://peps.python.org/pep-0735/)
[PEP 751 – A file format to record Python dependencies for installation reproducibility](https://peps.python.org/pep-0751/)

On the one hand, dependency groups are supposed to be coherent sets of dependencies that make sense as a specification of "things that should be installed simultaneously in at least some cases". They go beyond project extras and represent increased flexibility in pyproject.toml that can be useful for developers.

On the other hand, now we have lock files, and pip has experimental support for writing them and plans for installing from them. I generally agree that there are good reasons not to install directly from a list of *abstract, unresolved* dependencies given in a `pyproject.toml` file - even if that's exactly what you'd normally put directly on a pip command line.

What I'd like to see, therefore, is functionality to *generate a lockfile from a dependency group* (or from project dependencies or optional dependencies). Have the solver figure out what concrete dependencies are needed, and record them for later use. Then for people who do want to install directly from abstract dependencies, it would be more easily scriptable, without messing around with tools like `jq` etc. plus the lockfile itself would be a useful artifact.

I think we've drifted from the original issue here. The OP's report is that when the metadata is missing version data, an unhandled exception is raised. The resolution here is to handle the exception, and report a more informative message - *not* to try to recover from the problem. That was my mistake - in my response [here](https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/13443#issuecomment-3103394732) I was responding to your question "should we treat the Version field the same, by skipping over it silently, or raise a warning instead?", and I missed that you had omitted the important (and correct, IMO) third alternative, that we should not change the behaviour, and continue to produce an *error* here. It's just that the error needs to be more informative.

Given that, the behaviour of `pip freeze` and `pip list` is a side issue. What matters is that we catch the existing exception, and provide a meaningful message. That message needs to say that the version information in the metadata file is wrong, and help the user find the relevant file. So I'd suggest something like

> Invalid version data (XXX) in metadata file foo-1.0.dist-info/METADATA

Or "Missing version data in..." if the version is missing altogether. That gives the user the details of what the invalid value is, and where it's found, without getting bogged down in the question of whether the version in the `.dist-info` directory name is "correct" or not.

@ramannanda9 Unfortunately, that's not a good reason for pip to retain the legacy resolver. Being able to install a set of requirements that are incompatible was a *bug* in the legacy resolver, and supporting people who rely on that bug has never been a goal.

If projects want to continue using that capability, then at some point they will have to pin their version of pip.

> If projects want to continue using that capability, then at some point they will have to pin their version of pi

There are two other options for users with this use case:

* Write a script that installs each requirement one at a time. While pip is consistent on a single install command it does not try to make the install consistent with your existing environment and so installing one at a time is very similar to the legacy resolver (though be aware this behavior *may* change in the future).
* Use a different Python package installer, like uv or pdm, which have features to override requirements or provide your own dependency metadata for individual packages.

I have thought about the design of how constraints and build constraints would interact in pip, I have a branch that implements this but I still have a fair bit of work to add tests for this design.

I think the design is easiest presented in table form.

Here is the current state:

| Requirement Level | `PIP_CONSTRAINT` |  `--constraint` |
| --- | --- |--- |
| Install | Applied | Applied |
| Build | Applied | Not Applied |
| Build of Build (etc.)  | Applied | Not Applied |

And here would be the new state:

| Requirement Level | `PIP_CONSTRAINT` | `PIP_BUILD_CONSTRAINT` | `--constraint` | `--build-constraint` |
| --- | --- |--- |--- |--- |
| Install | Applied | Not Applied | Applied | Not Applied |
| Build | Applied unless overridden | Applied and overrides | Not Applied | Applied and overrides |
| Build of Build (etc.)  | Applied unless overridden | Applied and overrides | Not Applied | Not Applied (but overrides?) |

They key here is that `PIP_BUILD_CONSTRAINT` or  `--build-constraint`  would apply to the build environment overrides `PIP_CONSTRAINT` if it is set, on the assumption that if the user is passing one of these arguments they intend that to be the constraints for building, not `PIP_CONSTRAINT`.

Secondly I have modeled the current havior of `PIP_CONSTRAINT` /  `--constraint` with `PIP_BUILD_CONSTRAINT` / `--build-constraint`, in that `--build-constraint` is not passed recursively, but due to the nature of env variables `PIP_BUILD_CONSTRAINT`  applied to every subprocess of subprocess called. My thinking is that some users may have constraints on their direct build environment, but not on their build of their build environments, as that would be trickier to reason about, but they have an option to do so with `PIP_BUILD_CONSTRAINT`.

Finally there is the situation of `PIP_CONSTRAINT` and `--build-constraint`, this is a weird edge case, the user has a seperation of concerns of install and build constraints, but there is a build of a build. Should the presense of `--build-constraint` cause `PIP_CONSTRAINT` not to be applied in  the build of the build? I don't know, but I just realized this is how I've currently implemented it, and it pops out of this override design natrually, so it might be a bit messy to implement it in a different way.

There are a couple of other designs that would be simpler, but both would introduce at least minor backwards incompatibilities.

Passing `--constraint` and `--build-constraint` recursively:

| Requirement Level | `PIP_CONSTRAINT` / `--constraint`  | `PIP_BUILD_CONSTRAINT` / `--build-constraint` |
| --- | --- |--- |
| Install | Applied | Not Applied |
| Build | Applied unless overridden | Applied and overrides | 
| Build of Build (etc.)  | Applied unless overridden | Applied and overrides | 

Or not pass `PIP_CONSTRAINT` to the build environment and only allowing `PIP_BUILD_CONSTRAINT` to be applied recursively:

| Requirement Level | `PIP_CONSTRAINT` | `PIP_BUILD_CONSTRAINT` | `--constraint` | `--build-constraint` |
| --- | --- |--- |--- |--- |
| Install | Applied | Not Applied | Applied | Not Applied |
| Build | Not Applied | Applied | Not Applied | Applied |
| Build of Build (etc.)  | Not Applied | Applied | Not Applied | Not Applied |

FWIW I went with a design that somewhat breaks backwards compatibility, so you have to opt in by specifying `--build-constraint ...`  or `--use-feature=build-constraint` (the later is when you don't want `PIP_CONSTRAINT` to affect build constraints and you don't want to specify build constraints, which is actually impossible without this feature) until at least pip 26.1.
